# Forecasting

The theory stopped at the Wold decomposition. This chapter is about using it. The `forecast` package fits a model and returns a point forecast and a prediction interval. Once the package is installed, the function is left to choose the orders. Automatic selection evaluates candidate models by an information criterion, while autocorrelation plots remain useful for diagnosis and interpretation.

## Accidental deaths

`USAccDeaths` is a monthly count of accidental deaths in the United States, six years, $72$ months, ending in December 1978.{{cite:brockwell_davis1991}}{{cite:hyndman_athanasopoulos2021}}

![Monthly accidental deaths in the United States, 1973 to 1978. The series is not white noise: deaths are higher in the northern summer, and the level sags and then recovers.](../figures/deaths-series.pdf){#fig-deaths}

Plotting a series that R already knows is a time series puts time on the horizontal axis. @fig-deaths is not white noise. Deaths are higher in the middle of the year, the northern summer, and lower in winter. A twelve-month cycle is the obvious feature.{{cite:hyndman_athanasopoulos2021}} (§2.3, Time series patterns) The overall level is not a straight trend.{{cite:dodge2008}} (p. 536, Time Series) It sags and then recovers, a slow movement in the observed level whose cause needs separate evidence.

The autocorrelation and the partial autocorrelation both keep oscillating. An MA process would cut the autocorrelation off after a finite lag.{{cite:hyndman_athanasopoulos2021}} (Ch. 9, §9.4) An AR process would cut the partial autocorrelation off.{{cite:hyndman_athanasopoulos2021}} (Ch. 9, §9.3) Neither plot dies. That is the seasonality, still in the correlations.{{cite:hyndman_athanasopoulos2021}} (Ch. 9, §9.1)

Differencing at lag $12$,
$$
\nabla_{12} X_t=X_t-X_{t-12},
$$
removes a twelve-month cycle and, as a side effect, a linear trend. The differenced series still slopes. A linear trend left after a seasonal difference means the original series had a quadratic trend. One further difference at lag $1$ takes that slope out. What remains is closer to a constant mean and a constant scatter. The autocorrelation of that twice-differenced series still has a spike at the first lag, and a spike near one year. Those are the MA terms.

![Autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation, in months. The top row is the raw series: neither plot dies, and the year shows up at lags 12 and 24. The bottom row is the series after a seasonal difference and a first difference. What remains is a spike at lag 1 and a spike near lag 12.](../figures/deaths-corr.pdf){#fig-deaths-corr}

`auto.arima`, with the seasonal option left on, fits a seasonal ARIMA model, an autoregressive integrated moving average after differencing.{{cite:box_jenkins1970}}{{cite:hyndman_khandakar2008}} The series it receives is already monthly. The documentation of `USAccDeaths` describes monthly totals of accidental deaths in the United States, and it lists the first six months of 1979 apart from the series that is stored.{{cite:r_usaccdeaths_ah}} (Description) That stored object is a `ts` series of length $72$, from January 1973 through December 1978, with frequency $12$. Frequency $12$ means twelve observations in each year, and it is an attribute of the series. `auto.arima` reads the attribute. The call does not estimate a seasonal period, and it does not discover that the counts are monthly.
```r
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("forecast")
fit <- auto.arima(USAccDeaths, seasonal = TRUE)
fit
fc <- forecast(fit, h = 12)
fc$mean[1]
sum(fc$mean)
```
The model selected for this series is ARIMA$(0,1,1)(0,1,1)_{12}$ with no constant. It differences once at lag $12$, keeps a seasonal MA(1) on that lag, differences once more at lag $1$, and keeps an ordinary MA(1). There is no autoregressive term. Both moving-average coefficients are negative. A moving-average coefficient weights a lagged innovation, the one-step forecast error.{{cite:hyndman_athanasopoulos2021}} (Ch. 9, §9.4) It does not record a change in behaviour. Let $B$ denote the backshift operator, so that $BX_t=X_{t-1}$, and let $\varepsilon_t$ denote the innovation at time $t$. With no constant, the fitted equation is
$$
(1-B)(1-B^{12})X_t=(1+\theta B)(1+\Theta B^{12})\varepsilon_t,
$$
where $\theta$ is the ordinary moving-average coefficient and $\Theta$ is the seasonal coefficient.{{cite:hyndman_athanasopoulos2021}} (Ch. 9, §9.9) Expanding the right-hand side also places the product $\theta\Theta$ on $\varepsilon_{t-13}$. A negative $\Theta$ multiplies the innovation from twelve months earlier: a positive innovation contributes a negative amount, and a negative innovation contributes a positive amount. The sign is the sign of that weight. Taking the same sign as evidence that a worse year is followed by more careful conduct, or that a quieter year is followed by a slack one, treats a forecast error as a measurement of behaviour. The series records deaths. An innovation is the model's one-step error, not the change from one January to the next, and the fit contains no measurement of conduct.

The differences are fixed before AICc is computed. The default seasonal test measures seasonal strength and, for this series, sets one seasonal difference, $D=1$.{{cite:r_forecast_auto_arima_ah}} (Usage, argument seasonal.test; Details) The KPSS unit-root test is then applied to that seasonally differenced series and sets one ordinary difference, $d=1$.{{cite:r_forecast_auto_arima_ah}} (Usage, argument test) With $d$ and $D$ held fixed, the stepwise search minimises AICc over the autoregressive and moving-average orders only.{{cite:hyndman_athanasopoulos2021}} (Ch. 9, §9.6 and §9.9) It does not choose the differences. AICc is the small-sample correction of AIC. In `forecast::auto.arima` the argument `ic` defaults to `"aicc"`, the first value in `c("aicc", "aic", "bic")`.{{cite:r_forecast_auto_arima_ah}} (Usage, argument ic) AIC and BIC can be requested. Neither is the default. The missing constant is a restriction of the search. A drift term is admitted only when the total number of differences is one, and a mean only when the series is not differenced. This fit has one ordinary difference and one seasonal difference, so the candidates have no drift. The printed model has a coefficient for each moving-average term and no other coefficient.

![The forecast from January 1979. The darker band is the 80% interval and the lighter band is the 95% interval. The red point is the reported January total, 7798, inside the wider band and below the point forecast.](../figures/deaths-forecast.pdf){#fig-deaths-fc}

The fit uses the series through December 1978. One step ahead, the January 1979 point forecast is $8336$ deaths, the fitted mean rounded to the nearest death. @fig-deaths-fc is that forecast. The darker band is the 80% interval and the lighter band is the 95% interval. The documented January 1979 total is $7798$.{{cite:r_usaccdeaths_ah}} (Description) That count is not one of the seventy-two months used to fit the model. It lies below the point forecast, inside the 95% interval, and outside the 80% interval. The interval treats future innovations as Gaussian and leaves the uncertainty in the estimated coefficients out of the variance.{{cite:hyndman_athanasopoulos2021}} (Ch. 9, §9.8) It is a band for the fitted model. It does not establish that a counted death meant the same thing in 1979 as in the fitted years. The twelve point forecasts from January 1979 through December 1979 sum to $109{,}953$ after the monthly means are added and the total is rounded to the nearest death. That sum adds forecasts. It is not an observed annual total. The documentation records the first six months of 1979 and does not record a total for the year, so there is no reported 1979 annual count to place beside $109{,}953$.

The moving-average polynomial reaches lag $13$. Once the horizon is past that lag, every innovation on the right-hand side lies in the future, and the point forecast sets future innovations to zero.{{cite:hyndman_athanasopoulos2021}} (Ch. 9, §9.8) The forecast then satisfies
$$
(1-B)(1-B^{12})\hat X_{n+h}=0.
$$
Equivalently, the first differences repeat every twelve months,
$$
\hat X_{n+h}-\hat X_{n+h-1}=\hat X_{n+h-12}-\hat X_{n+h-13}.
$$
The level therefore changes by the same amount from one year to the next in every calendar month. The path is a straight line plus a seasonal pattern. A quadratic is a different path. For $X_t=ct^2$,
$$
(1-B)(1-B^{12})X_t=24c,
$$
a nonzero constant whenever $c\neq 0$. Carrying that constant would require a drift on the twice-differenced scale. This fit has no drift, so the long-run point forecast does not follow a quadratic. The same distinction, in a non-seasonal model, is the degree of the polynomial: a constant together with $d$ differences produces a forecast polynomial of degree $d$, and omitting the constant produces degree $d-1$.{{cite:hyndman_athanasopoulos2021}} (Ch. 9, §9.7) A short-range forecast still depends on the latest innovations through the moving-average terms. Once the horizon passes lag $13$, those innovations no longer enter the forecast equation directly. They still set the level, the slope and the seasonal pattern of the path that equation leaves behind. Holding the estimated coefficients fixed, and adding $500$ to the December 1978 count, raises the point forecast forty-eight months ahead by $892$ deaths. That comparison does not refit the coefficients. What the forecast equation itself retains is the linear-plus-seasonal mean structure.

The call passes no period of its own. Frequency $12$ is already stored on `USAccDeaths`, and the seasonal difference and the seasonal moving average use that period. In the stepwise search, AICc chooses only the autoregressive and moving-average orders. The seasonal-strength test and the KPSS unit-root test have already fixed $D=1$ and $d=1$, and the period is the frequency the series already carries.

## A hundred minutes of traffic

`WWWusage` counts hits on a server, one number per minute for $100$ minutes. There is no season in a series that short.

![Server hits, one number per minute. The autocorrelation dies slowly and then changes sign, because the series wanders. The partial autocorrelation is essentially one spike, at lag 1.](../figures/www-series.pdf){#fig-www}

The autocorrelation in @fig-www dies slowly. The partial autocorrelation dies after a lag or two. After one ordinary difference the series is closer to a flat mean, and `auto.arima` selects an ARMA(1,1) on that difference:
```r
need <- function(pkg) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pkg, character.only = TRUE))
}
need("forecast")
auto.arima(WWWusage, seasonal = TRUE)
```
The fit has no seasonal piece: one difference, one autoregressive coefficient, and one moving-average coefficient. Both coefficients are positive. A busy minute is followed by a busy minute, and a minute that was busy relative to the minute before it is followed by a minute that is busier still. That is a trend, of the sort a topic has when it is spreading, and it does not need a separate time covariate.

![A twenty-minute forecast for the server traffic. The point forecast is nearly flat. The interval widens as the horizon moves away.](../figures/www-forecast.pdf){#fig-www-fc}

The forecast of the next minutes, in @fig-www-fc, is a shallow line, and the interval widens as the horizon moves away. At a long horizon the forecast has forgotten the local level and sits on the mean that the difference implies.

## What this chapter does not cover

Autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity, and its generalisations, put a time-series model on the variance rather than only on the mean.{{cite:engle2001_garch101}} (§ “ARCH/GARCH Models”){{cite:bollerslev1986}} (§2, pp. 308–310) The conditional variance responds to past squared shocks and, in GARCH, past conditional variances. Count-valued series require a sampling model on nonnegative integers, rather than an unrestricted Gaussian observation model.

## Exercises

1. A linear trend, differenced at lag $12$, leaves a constant. A quadratic trend, differenced at lag $12$, leaves a linear trend. Explain why, for $X_t=a+bt+ct^2$, the seasonal difference $X_t-X_{t-12}$ still depends on $t$.

2. Both moving-average coefficients in the accidental-death model are negative. What does the seasonal coefficient multiply, and how does its sign enter the contribution of the innovation from twelve months earlier?

3. Why is exponentiating a forecast made on the log scale not the same object as a forecast of the mean on the original scale?

4. The call `auto.arima(USAccDeaths, seasonal = TRUE)` passes no period as a separate argument. What supplies the seasonal period, and where does that period appear in the selected model?
